activities.caption: rebuild the chain from a single hop to a design rule
activities.name: htFickOrder

config.prompt: From one atomic hop to a carburising budget — drag the chain into order:
items: An atom swaps with a vacancy, or squeezes between lattice sites
Each hop is one step of a random walk — biased down the concentration gradient
The result is a flux proportional to the gradient: J = −D·(dC/dx)
Left alone, the gradient itself smooths with time (Fick's second law)
Its solutions give the working rule: penetration depth grows as √(Dt)
config.why: Quadruple the furnace hold and the case deepens only twofold — every carburising schedule is that square root, priced in hours.

activities.anchor: kilns compete over tens of degrees
activities.caption: one line of the furnace note misreads the exponential
activities.name: htArrheniusSpot

config.prompt: A process note on diffusivity — one line is wrong. Click it:
lines: Diffusivity obeys D = D₀·exp(−Q/RT): every hop must clear an energy barrier.
For carbon in austenite, D₀ ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s with Q ≈ 148 kJ/mol.
Raising the furnace from 900 °C to 1000 °C roughly triples D.
A quench cools through hundreds of degrees in seconds, cutting diffusion to about half its furnace rate.
That exponential sensitivity is why furnace builders fight over tens of degrees.
config.correction: A quench does not halve diffusion — it effectively stops atomic motion mid-flight. Exponential sensitivity cuts both ways: modest heating multiplies hops enormously, and rapid cooling suppresses them almost completely.
config.why: The same exponential that makes kilns fight over degrees is what lets a water tank freeze a microstructure in place.

activities.anchor: Every treatment is a path drawn on this map
activities.caption: put the nose of the C-curve on the temperature axis
activities.name: htNosePlace

config.prompt: For eutectoid steel, transformation is fastest at the nose of the C. Place it on the temperature axis:
config.why: Near 550 °C. Above it the driving force is small; below it diffusion crawls — the race is only lost in the middle, which is why a quench must outrun that one spot.

activities.caption: call the quench's peak hardness before the temper
activities.name: htQuenchEstimate

config.prompt: The 0.8 % C shaft ends at 45 HRC after tempering and 20 HRC furnace-cooled. At its hardest — straight out of the water quench, before tempering — roughly what hardness did it touch?
config.why: About 65 HRC: full martensite, carbon trapped in a distorted BCT lattice — and maximum thermal stress, which is why high-carbon grades are the ones that quench-crack. The temper then settles it to 45 HRC.
config.context: Same alloy, 20 → 65 → 45 HRC: chemistry never moved, only the itinerary.

activities.caption: true or false — three itineraries, one vocabulary audit
activities.name: htMisconceptionJudge

statements.s: Annealing, normalising and tempering are three names for the same operation — making steel softer.
statements.why: Anneal = reset to full equilibrium; normalise = air-cooled grain cleanup; temper = partial retreat from martensite. Different itineraries, different targets.

statements.s: Tempering a normalised steel accomplishes nothing, because there is no martensite to relax.
statements.why: The temper's whole job is relieving trapped martensite — no martensite, no settlement to negotiate.

statements.s: Quenching hardens steel because cooling quickly itself adds strength.
statements.why: Speed adds nothing on its own. The quench works by preventing diffusion, so metastable martensite can form that equilibrium would never allow.

statements.s: Cool the same steel too slowly and you get soft pearlite no matter how dramatically the water boils.
statements.why: Only paths that outrun the nose of the C-curve escape to martensite.

activities.anchor: the discipline of hitting the peak
activities.caption: file each airframe condition by its ageing recipe
activities.name: htTemperBuckets

config.prompt: The spec sheet's T-temper is an ageing recipe — file each condition:

items.label: solution-treated, quenched, then held at room temperature
GP zones and θ″/θ′ plates at peak spacing

config.why: T4 means solution-treated and naturally aged; T6 means solution-treated and artificially aged. Hold too long or too hot past either peak and the precipitates coarsen — strength falls again.

activities.caption: pair each surface treatment with its signature
activities.name: htCaseMatch

config.prompt: Four ways to harden only the surface — pair each with its mechanism:

pairs.right: carbon seeps inward at ~900–950 °C, then quench-and-temper hardens only the carbon-rich skin
nitrogen at ~500 °C, below transformation temperature — minimal distortion, for precision work
no chemistry at all — heat only the surface past transformation, quench before the core notices
thick insulation on the spine, bare steel at the edge — hard edge, tough spine, visible hamon

config.why: All four give surface and bulk different jobs: a wear-resistant case over a shock-absorbing core. The Japanese smiths ran the experiment centuries before the vocabulary existed.

config.root: The violence budget: every quench is thermal shock, and half of heat-treatment engineering moderates the other half.

start.text: A batch of high-carbon parts keeps quench-cracking in plain water — which cools fast through the nose and fast again exactly where martensite forms. What do you change?

choices.label: Switch to a quenchant tuned: fast through the nose, slow below martensite start
choices.feedback: Oil, salt and polymer quenchants exist precisely to run that order — the reverse of plain water.

choices.label: Interrupt the quench — pull the part out above martensite start and hold
choices.feedback: Austempering and martempering: bend the schedule instead of the part.

choices.label: Quench harder in brine to get it over with
choices.feedback: Faster through the nose — and faster again through martensite start, exactly where the cracking lives.

tuned.text: A tuned quenchant races past the nose (where pearlite waits) then cools gently past martensite start. Press quenching holds geometry; a cryogenic trip below finishes retained austenite on purpose.

interrupted.text: Held above martensite start, the section equalises before transformation begins — thermal gradients that would have cracked the part never get built. The transformation then runs at low stress.

brine.text: The fastest route to full martensite is also the fastest route to quench cracks: the surface contracts around a hot core, and the stresses warp or split the part. Speed was never the cure here.

config.why: Cooling rate is a curve to be shaped, not a number to maximise — fast where the nose waits, gentle where martensite forms.
